methods.label: Count one complete motion cycle
methods.explanation:
The motion repeats, so we can count one common cycle. We must distinguish an interior pass from a meeting at a wall, where the swimmers can turn together without exchanging order.

The faster swimmer completes a round trip in \(180/3=60\) seconds, and the slower swimmer in \(180/2=90\) seconds. After \(180\) seconds both have returned to their respective starting ends and begin moving in their original directions. Since
\[
12\cdot60=720=4\cdot180,
\]
there are four identical cycles.

Measure position in feet from the faster swimmer's starting end. Let \(d(t)\) be the faster swimmer's position minus the slower swimmer's position after \(t\) seconds in the first cycle. Initially \(d(0)=-90\). Between turns, \(d\) changes at the difference of their signed velocities. For example, before the first turn it increases at \(3+2=5\) feet per second. Accounting for all turns gives
\[
d(t)=\begin{cases}
5t-90,&0\le t\le30,\\
90-t,&30\le t\le45,\\
270-5t,&45\le t\le60,\\
t-90,&60\le t\le90,\\
90-t,&90\le t\le120,\\
5t-630,&120\le t\le135,\\
t-90,&135\le t\le150,\\
810-5t,&150\le t\le180.
\end{cases}
\]
A meeting occurs exactly when \(d(t)=0\). Solving these linear equations and retaining roots in their stated intervals gives the distinct times
\[
18,\ 54,\ 90,\ 126,\ 162
\]
seconds. The intervals cover the entire cycle, so there are no other meetings. The shared endpoint \(t=90\) is counted once. At cycle boundaries the swimmers are at opposite ends, so multiplying the cycle count introduces no duplicate events.

At \(t=90\), both swimmers reach the far wall. Just before and just after this time, \(d(t)<0\), so they do not exchange order. At each of the other four meetings, \(d\) changes sign and the swimmers pass in the interior.

Consequently, counting every meeting, including shared wall turns, gives \(4\cdot5=\boxed{20}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\). Counting only strict interior passes gives \(4\cdot4=\boxed{16}\), which is absent from the choices. The wording leaves this distinction unresolved.
